summary.text: A functional group is a substituent or moiety in a molecule that causes the molecule's characteristic chemical reactions.
The same functional group undergoes the same or similar reactions regardless of the rest of the molecule, which lets chemists predict reactions and design syntheses.
Functional groups also shape solubility: under the rule 'like dissolves like', sugar dissolves in water because both share the hydroxyl group.

items.prompt: Sugar stirs into a glass of water and disappears. Which idea about molecules best explains it?

options.label: Sugar is a solid, so it can only break apart where water is a gas
Water molecules are smaller, so sugar fits between them without bonding
Both carry the same kind of group, and those groups attract each other strongly
Both are nonpolar molecules, and nonpolar molecules mix with everything

items.explain: 'Like dissolves like': sugar and water share the hydroxyl group, and hydroxyls interact strongly with each other.

items.prompt: A chemist meets a huge, unfamiliar molecule that contains a group she knows well. What should she expect from that group?

options.label: Similar reactions to those it undergoes elsewhere, though nearby groups can shift it
Exactly the same reactions, with nothing nearby able to change them
Reactions she cannot predict until the whole molecule is studied
No reactions at all, because the rest of the molecule is too large

items.explain: A functional group reacts the same or similarly regardless of the rest of the molecule, but nearby functional groups can modify its reactivity.

items.prompt: A chemist calls the left half of a molecule a moiety. How does a moiety relate to a functional group?

options.label: A moiety is always exactly one functional group
A moiety can be one functional group or a larger unit made of several
A moiety is the part of a molecule that has no functional groups
A moiety is any charged group, like a carboxylate salt's group

items.explain: A moiety is an entire 'half' of a molecule, which can be a single functional group or a larger unit of several.

items.prompt: A molecule that barely mixes with water gains a group more electronegative than the atoms it attaches to. What happens to the molecule?

options.label: It stays unable to mix with water
It turns charged and so splits into two separate molecules
It becomes a ligand and so binds to a central atom
It becomes polar and so soluble in some aqueous environment

items.explain: Groups more electronegative than their attachment atoms become polar, which makes otherwise nonpolar molecules polar and soluble in some aqueous environment.

items.prompt: Sulfur sits just below oxygen on the periodic table, yet sulfur compounds behave in their own way. What ability explains this?

options.label: Sulfur is lighter than oxygen, so it moves more freely
Sulfur can form more bonds than oxygen
Sulfur cannot bond to carbon at all, unlike oxygen
Sulfur carries a partially filled octet, so it acts as an acid

items.explain: Compounds containing sulfur show unique chemistry due to sulfur's ability to form more bonds than oxygen, its lighter analogue.

items.prompt: A chemist compares an iodoalkane with a fluoroalkane. Which has the more stable carbon–halogen bond?

options.label: The iodoalkane
Neither; haloalkane bonds are all equally stable
The fluoroalkane
Neither; haloalkanes have no carbon–halogen bond

items.explain: The carbon–halogen bond can be relatively weak, as in an iodoalkane, or quite stable, as in a fluoroalkane.

paragraphs.heading: What a functional group is
paragraphs.text: A functional group is a set of atoms within a molecule that causes the molecule's typical chemical reactions. Its chemical properties are distinctive whatever the other atoms in the molecule happen to be. Covalent bonds hold the group's atoms together and tie them to the rest of the molecule.

paragraphs.heading: Why chemists care
paragraphs.text: A given functional group undergoes the same or similar reactions no matter what the rest of the molecule is made of. That lets chemists predict how compounds will react and behave, and design ways to make them. Other functional groups nearby can change a group's reactivity, though. In retrosynthetic analysis, a way of planning organic synthesis, converting one functional group into another is a useful tool.

paragraphs.heading: Like dissolves like
paragraphs.text: Specific interactions between functional groups also cause complexation and solvation. In the rule of thumb like dissolves like, it is groups that are shared or that interact well with each other that make one substance dissolve in another. Sugar dissolves in water because both carry the hydroxyl group, −OH, and hydroxyls interact strongly with each other. When a group is more electronegative than the atom it is attached to, it becomes polar, and an otherwise nonpolar molecule carrying it becomes polar and can dissolve in some watery settings.

paragraphs.heading: Charges, ligands and polymers
paragraphs.text: Functional groups can carry a charge, as in carboxylate salts (−COO⁻); the molecule then becomes a polyatomic or complex ion. When groups bind to the central atom of a coordination complex, they are called ligands. In the repeating units of polymers, functional groups attach to a nonpolar core of carbon atoms and so give carbon chains chemical character.

paragraphs.heading: Naming by group
paragraphs.text: Systematic names for organic compounds come from combining functional group names with the names of the parent alkanes. In traditional naming, the first carbon after the one attached to the group is the alpha carbon, then come beta, gamma and so on. So in gamma-aminobutyric acid, the amine sits on the third carbon of the chain attached to the carboxylic acid group. IUPAC conventions use numbers for positions instead, giving 4-aminobutanoic acid. Traditional names also label isomers with qualifiers: isopropanol, or propan-2-ol, is an isomer of n-propanol, or propan-1-ol.

paragraphs.heading: Families of groups
paragraphs.text: In written formulas, R and R' usually stand for an attached hydrogen or for a hydrocarbon side chain, which can be any length. Hydrocarbons are defined by groups called hydrocarbyls that contain only carbon and hydrogen and differ in the number and order of double bonds, and each kind reacts differently. Haloalkanes are defined by a carbon–halogen bond, which is fairly weak in an iodoalkane and quite stable in a fluoroalkane. Apart from fluorinated compounds, haloalkanes readily undergo substitution or elimination reactions.

paragraphs.heading: Oxygen, sulfur, phosphorus, boron
paragraphs.text: Compounds with C–O bonds react differently depending on where the bond is and its hybridization: the oxygen in carbonyl groups withdraws electrons, while the oxygen in alcohol groups donates them. Sulfur can form more bonds than oxygen, its lighter relative on the periodic table, and phosphorus can form more than nitrogen, which gives both their own chemistry. Boron compounds have partly filled octets, so they act as Lewis acids.

paragraphs.heading: Groups and moieties
paragraphs.text: The word moiety partly overlaps with functional group. A moiety, though, is a whole half of a molecule, which can be one functional group or a larger unit made of several. An aryl moiety, for example, can be any group that contains an aromatic ring, however many functional groups it has.
